interest: Shows postwar Japan purging militarist language from forestry law while SCAP surveys northern Honshu's wartime-strained lumber industry.
overview: This file contains State Department records from decimal file 894.6171 dating from December 1945 to November 1946, comprising diplomatic despatches from the Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo to the Secretary of State in Washington, along with Japanese legislative records and technical reports from General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ/SCAP). Despatch No. 88 (December 10, 1945) transmits an English translation of Diet Bill No. IV, amending the wartime forestry cultivation law by excising militarist terminology related to the 'Greater East Asia War' and adjusting legal obligations surrounding afforestation bonds. Despatch No. 716 (November 20, 1946) forwards Report No. 58 of the SCAP Natural Resources Section, titled 'The Forestry Situation in Northern Honshu' (October 10, 1946), prepared by 1st Lt. W. T. Nearn. This extensive survey assesses forest ownership, standing timber volume, administrative structures, silvicultural systems, logging methods, and industrial output (lumber, charcoal, ties, mine props, and pulpwood) across Aomori, Iwate, Miyagi, Akita, and Yamagata prefectures, highlighting critical postwar recovery challenges including food shortages, transport bottlenecks, and equipment deficits.

subfiles.summary: Prepared by 1st Lt. W. T. Nearn, this comprehensive report assesses the forestry sector across Aomori, Iwate, Miyagi, Akita, and Yamagata prefectures, which together encompass over 8.3 million acres of forest land holding more than 9.2 billion cubic feet of timber. It outlines the administrative structure of the Japanese Bureau of Forestry, regional offices (eirinkyoku), and prefectural forestry offices, recommending administrative unification and improved management planning for private holdings. It examines silvicultural treatments, hand-logging techniques, kimma sleds, forest railways, and river rafting down the Yoneshiro River to the large sawmills at Noshiro. The survey provides detailed statistical tables spanning 1935–1946 for lumber, charcoal, railroad ties, mine props, and pulpwood, while identifying key production constraints including rural food shortages, transportation deficits, and shortages of replacement saw blades and lubricants caused by wartime bombing of urban factories.
subfiles.title: Natural Resources Section Report No. 58: The Forestry Situation in Northern Honshu (A Preliminary Report)
